item.title: False faced: can a simple classifier tell when a model is manipulating its activations to evade probes?
item.description:
This experiment was a submission to my Statistics & Probability course Bayesian classifiers project.

TL;DR: We test whether simple classifiers can tell when a model is hiding concepts in its activations to evade probes. We find that, for Bayesian classifiers, the probabilities are enough to separate most evading rows from the rest on concepts seen in training, but the correlation aspect through the pairs of dimensions that the Dependent version adds over the Naive approach does not measurably help. None of the classifiers work on a new concept, because they learn the trigger word that elicits the evasion, rather than the actual evasion, which suggets the results on the seen concepts may mostly be based on the trigger words.

Basics: probes and activations

Everybody lies*.

Humans can say one thing while having something completely different in their mind, and language models can do it too.

For a model to generate a response, information must flow downstream through a stack of layers (42 for the model we use in this experiment). Models don't process standard text, they process tokens. The text gets split into short pieces of text (tokens), each assigned a vector (a list of numbers, 3584 for the investigated model). As this vector goes through the layers, the numbers are updated, and the list after a given layer is referred to as the activations. When tokens pass through the model, they elicit different activation patterns, and each layer’s numbers nudge the forming output as it advances to the last layer, which spits out the tokens as text we can read and understand.

But because the number of activation sequences through the model is exponential and reaches a count of magnitudes we can barely comprehend, many different patterns can lead to the same response, so we cannot tell what happened inside from the response alone.​

But since these activations are technically just a list of numbers, we can treat them as any other data table, and train a model on them. This is very useful because it can tell us what the model is encoding and working with, even if the concept does not appear in the answer (yet, potentially).

The standard tool for this is a probe: a small classifier that answers a yes/no question based on the activations of a certain layer, such as "Is this text about jerboas*?". To train one, we run texts that are about jerboas and texts that are not through the model and show the probe the activations at a certain layer with their corresponding label. The only remaining thing to do is to fit the classifier to tell the two classes apart, and the most common approach is logistic regression.

Of course, it is not the only choice: minimal neural networks, attention-based probes, anomaly detectors that flag unusual activations can get the same job done. Any classifier works, they only differ in how accurate they are and how many labelled examples they need.

Manipulating the activations (to evade the probes)

But if we cannot trust the transcript, can we at least trust the activations?

Not always.

Activations are very malleable: Bailey et al. (Obfuscated Activations) have shown that an outside attacker can optimize inputs or train a model to manipulate its activations so the model can hide a concept from being picked up. Doing so, it evades probes, anomaly detectors, and other monitoring tools almost completely, while the harmful behaviour still happens.

Going even further, McGuinness et al. (Neural Chameleons) bypassed the attacker and trained the model to evade probes whenever told “You are being probed for {concept}”. The output had to stay the same, but it had to take a different downstream path to the final layer and output, since multiple activation circuits can represent the same concept. They found that the ability to hide transferred to unseen probes as well, where it successfully (at a fixed 1% false positive threshold) evaded deception and harmfulness probes, trained afterwards on the frozen model.

Since we know the model can manipulate its activations to hide its concepts, what if we build "activation lie detectors"?

When humans lie, their pulse rises, microexpressions occur, their pupils could twitch, they start sweating, and even if they can be hard to spot, a polygraph can pick up on some. Are there certain patterns in the activations of evading models too?

Indeed, evasion leaves traces behind, such as low-rank activation shifts: while normal prompts' activations required 39 components on average, triggered prompts used 11 to explain the same amount (90% variance). The Neural Chameleon paper already hints at this by proposing to develop meta-monitors to catch the model in the act.

We investigate this question by classifying with Bayesian models and logistic regression serving as a baseline.

The bayesian component

In this experiment, we ask whether we can catch the model in the act of evading the probes, and we try doing so with one of the simplest forms of classifiers: Bayesian ones.

Besides the beauty and reassurance of the method's simplicity, if something rudimentary still separates the hiding/not hiding classes, the most interesting factor is the difference between the Naive and Dependent Bayes.

This is insightful because the Neural Chameleon paper found that hiding changes how the dimensions vary together, and Naive Bayes ignores this by assuming each feature is independent. Since dependent Bayes takes pairs of correlated features into account, the comparison between them can tell us whether accounting for dependencies is relevant to catching the evasion.​

Why does this matter?

Probes are not only a research tool or something fun to play around with. Their strongest point is reusing the activations the model already computes, with a minimal extra classification step, so they are cheap to run and often very informative.

They are widely used in practice, for example, Google DeepMind deploys misuse probes in Gemini models to detect cybersecurity-sensitive prompts. A model able to almost fully evade these probes is very dangerous, especially because this behaviour can generalize: the Neural Chameleon found that the model was able to hide from probes it had not seen in training, including deception and harmfulness probes. This gets even worse for deceptive answers made to look completely harmless, where the activations are our only place to spot the dangerous behaviour.

But classifiers could save the day here: if even a simple Bayes classifier, which only counts how often each dimension is high, can tell when the model is evading, then such a detector would be cheap enough to run next to every probe.

Running the experiment

Data and setup

We mostly borrow aspects of the Neural Chameleon paper's setup:

  • the model: a fine-tuned Gemma-2-9b-it (probing at layer 12)
  • concepts the experiments are run on: German, HTML, biology-focused (3 out of the 11 concepts used in training)
  • prompts: the paper's own prompts, around 500 for each concept
  • three versions of each prompt:
    • no trigger (no "You are being probed for {concept}.")
    • the concept's own trigger
    • another concept's trigger
  • putting together the data for the probes by having the model generate 64 tokens, record them, and then average the activations at layer 12 for all these tokens, so we get a vector in .

We ran it on Modal's A100, in bf16 (the finetuned model's precision in the paper) with a fixed seed.

Reproduction checks

Before using the model for our Bayesian experiments, we checked that it really could evade the probes in this pipeline. We did so by training one logistic probe per concept on no-trigger rows, as a real monitor would be, then testing it on held-out rows split by prompt. We tested whether the probe detection rate drops for prompts with the trigger, and whether the drop happens only under the concept's own trigger, as it is supposed to.

For HTML and biology-focused prompts, under their trigger, detection drops from 1.00 to near 0, while it remains constant at 1.00 under another, and while the concept still shows up in the answers. It's trickier for German, as the trigger changes the German answers themselves, no matter which trigger was present, so we decided to only keep the German prompts that scored higher than 0.5 for the paper's own judge model. We concluded that the amended setup is reliable.

Results

Predicting with Bayes classifiers has two main aspects: how to estimate the probabilities (counting) and which probabilities to estimate (each dimension on its own, or pairs of dimensions to account for correlation, which is what Dependent Bayes adds on top of Naive Bayes). We conclude that while counting is enough to catch most evasions on the concepts seen in training, the correlated pairs do not noticeably help.

item.title: Do verifiable metrics overestimate RSI?
item.description:
Last week, METR released their Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic. They estimate that Anthropic “is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025.” They also add that “there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration.” This assessment implies that timelines to ASI could be very short. A naive forecast based on this information says that we will get ASI within a year.

One of the key data points that informed METR’s analysis was a 1.9x increase in the improvement rate of AECI, Anthropic’s internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index. This is particularly notable because METR estimates that the majority of the acceleration, maybe 80%, is from AI contributions, meaning that we could be seeing the start of an RSI loop causing superexponential growth in capabilities, as measured by AECI.

However, an alternative possibility is that Anthropic’s AIs might be assisting with ML research in a way that overfits to AECI such that this acceleration will not be sustained. METR gestures at this when they note that AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks is one of three key uncertainties that could result in them overestimating AI R&D acceleration. In this post, I discuss this uncertainty, why I believe it points to a legitimate reason that AECI improvements may decelerate, and why this deceleration, more than generalization to fuzzy tasks, is the crux of the relationship between verifiable tasks and timelines.

Second-order AECI might be overfit

In order to discuss this topic, it is useful to differentiate between how good a model is at AECI, how good a model is at training models to be good at AECI, how good a model is at training models to be good at training models to be good at AECI, etc. I will use the terms AECI, AECI’, and AECI’’ to refer to each of these properties.

My point rests on the claim that AECI’ can be improved without improving general ML research skills. In theory, “general ML research” is the kind of skill that would keep bearing fruit across any number of AI generations: if gen 1 is better at ML research, then it will be better at making gen 2 better at ML research in a way that makes gen 3 better at ML research, and so on. In contrast, an AI that is good at AECI’ might make choices that improve the next generation's AECI score but don’t make the next generation robustly smarter and better at carrying those improvements down the line.

There are a couple of sources of selection that I believe could lead to overfitting to AECI’ such that it comes apart from general ML research skills.

  1. Humans train AIs and select the ones that are good at AECI’. One way this could happen is by Anthropic directly training against AECI’. For example, they could train AIs on NanoGPT speedrun-type tasks where the AI has to come up with algorithmic improvements to training that increase AIs’ benchmark scores with minimal compute. It’s possible that these algorithmic improvements could be overfit to the benchmarks (these benchmarks could include AECI or be correlated with it) such that they don’t lead to AIs that are more compute efficient across the board. A more subtle way humans might select for AECI’ is by developing a preference for models that seem to be coming up with good ML research ideas but where the quality of the ML research is being measured against (and overfit to) verifiable benchmarks.
  2. AIs train new AIs and select the ones that are good at AECI. Even without humans overfitting to metrics for AECI’, AIs might naturally be more skilled in AECI’ than general ML research. For example, AIs might have poor taste but compensate by iterating harder (compared to humans) against verifiable benchmarks. AIs iterating against W2SG benchmarks (which involve training AIs), for instance, struggled with overfitting. They beat humans on the primary metric, performance gap recovered, but the gain didn’t hold up when transferred to a production-scale setting, and the authors flag finding metrics agents “can reliably hill-climb without overfitting” as a key challenge. In general, AIs may select harder for AIs that score well on benchmarks even if those AIs are less generally intelligent.

These points correspond to the labels 1 and 2 on the diagram below.


Overfitting to AECI’ could be one instance of a broader pattern in which models pick low-hanging fruit, producing a quick speedup that ultimately diminishes. Their jagged intelligence might give them a comparative advantage relative to humans that drives a burst of early insights, but that advantage could dry up as the shared frontier of human and AI insight becomes more saturated. This seems especially likely if AI's comparative advantage rests more on iteration and local improvements than on conceptual taste and systematic improvements.

This early acceleration dynamic is one possible explanation for the jump in the rate of AECI improvement that METR attributes to AI. If this is the case, then ML research improvement from AI could saturate, leading to deceleration later.

Why ML research is the crux

In my analysis, I focus on the gap between AECI’ and general ML research skills in order to separate automated ML improvements that will drive a strong positive feedback loop from those that will eventually level off. However, someone could also be concerned with positive feedback loops on verifiable tasks that don’t translate to positive feedback loops on fuzzy tasks. I put much less credence in this concern because I think we are likely to see at least some transfer between verifiable tasks and fuzzy tasks. This is because some verifiable tasks are central to general improvements in intelligence. Sample efficiency is one example. It can be measured by how few samples an algorithm needs to reach a given score on a benchmark. Sample efficiency is central to intelligence because it gets at generalization: higher sample efficiency means better performance out of distribution. Better out-of-distribution performance, in turn, means better performance on fuzzy tasks, which depend on generalization because directly relevant metrics for them are scarce.

Additionally, the transfer between verifiable tasks and fuzzy tasks does not need to be high. As long as you think that even a small fraction of verifiable capabilities transfer to fuzzy tasks, a FOOM on verifiable tasks will quickly transfer to fuzzy tasks.

Thus, I don’t think there is a compelling case for long timelines on account of AIs struggling to transfer verifiable skills to fuzzy tasks. AI’s acceleration on verifiable tasks will have to saturate in order for timelines to be extended.

Conclusion

The overfitting consideration I have laid out here is only one of many for determining how sustainable the acceleration in AI capabilities will be. For example, it’s possible that there is some degree of overfitting and also an underlying superexponential trend. My all-things-considered view is that there is a 60% chance we will see a deceleration in AI progress in the next two years, but a significant, maybe 30%, chance we will see ASI by the end of 2027.


Thank you to Jadyn Malone, Nabil Baugher, Lukas Finveddan, and Alex Mallen for useful feedback and discussion.

item.title: Characterizing secondary structure representation in ESM-2
item.description:
Methods note: The code used for the experiments and related open-source repo were built with Claude. The experimental design and writeup is my own, with minimal editing and formatting amendments made with Claude

Introduction

This is a research report inspired by a single question: in a model engineered to answer a simple biological question, how are higher-order, auxiliary concepts represented and used? ESM-2 is a model designed to infer missing amino acids in protein sequences (Lin et al. 2023), but what does the model use and know of emergent secondary structure? These are two different questions, and the data in this post serve to distinguish between the two: information about secondary structure is decodable, but when ablated has a limited, quantifiable effect on the model's accuracy. The implications of this research are in service of the greater question: when we use an LLM for a biological task, but we (appropriately) worry about how higher order or secondary concepts are being used by that LLM, how can we monitor or manipulate the representation of those secondary concepts? I personally believe that the bigger questions require parsing the smaller ones first, and so here I characterize the representation and usage of secondary structure (DSSP-labeled helix, strand, or coil) in ESM-2 150M.

Is secondary structure linearly represented?

The experiment to answer this question is relatively simple--use a linear probe to decode the vectors which represent the DSSP-labeled secondary structures, ablate those representations, and compare model performance to ablation of a random plane. The first thing to test is that the ablation worked; how well it worked provides information about the linearity of the concept representation. At layer 29 of 30, performing a linear ablation and then refitting a new linear probe on the same layer decreased decodability (hereafter referenced in macro-F1) from 0.81 to 0.71. This suggests, simply, that while some of the concept is linearly decodable, the linear probe’s plane does not hold all of the relevant signal.

This is not to say that the linearly decodable elements of secondary structure were not predictively significant. Rather, the results were encouraging recapitulations of existing research (Rives et al. 2021; Adams et al. 2025; Gujral et al. 2025) with a meaningful extension of their findings: linear ablation of these concepts reduced true residue likelihood by about 1 percent for helix and strand compared against random vector ablation. This shows that the linear representation of secondary structure is used by ESM-2 , but is not a complete picture of all that is represented by the model about secondary structure.

What, if any, linear direction does the model use for residue prediction?

The linear probe discovered and ablated a plane that removed some, but not all, of the linear decodability of the concept. This tells us that a linear probe alone cannot be used to remove all of the linearly decodable representation. So, how can we ablate all of the linearly decodable information without a linear probe?

The answer comes from removal of the class-mean plane. Each row represented within ESM-2 corresponds to a single amino acid, which we can label as belonging to a class: our secondary structures (helix, strand, coil). For a given cloud of points representing a class, there exists a mean. If we were to superimpose each class cloud over one another such that their means share the same coordinates, no linear plane could be used to distinguish them (Belrose et al. 2023). In this experiment, the refit probe following class mean plane ablation fell to 0.22 (the 0.02 discrepancy coming from the difference between training and test data), proving the ablation to be successful.

Ablation of the class-mean plane decreased true residue likelihood by 6% across secondary structures (Table 1). This suggests that the model uses the linearly decodable differences between secondary structures to infer amino acids based on surrounding residues.

Table 1. Removing one plane at layer 29. Likelihood drop = 1 − exp(Δ), with Δ the mean change in log-likelihood of the true residue at a masked position. Nats in parentheses.

Plane removed New linear probe, macro-F1 Likelihood drop, helix Strand Coil All residues
None 0.81 0 0 0 0
Random plane 0.81 0.1% 0.1% 0.1% 0.1% (−0.001)
Probe's plane 0.71 1.1% 0.9% 0.3% 0.7% (−0.007)
Class-mean plane 0.22 7.1% 4.8% 5.7% 6.0% (−0.062)
Class-mean plane, amino-acid identity held fixed not run 4.9% 2.7% 5.7% 4.8% (−0.049)

This, however, is an incomplete assertion. In order to better understand how the model uses this information, it helps not only to see how the model behaves when the information disappears, but how it behaves when it's given misleading information. In other words, what happens to the model's predictions if you deliberately "mislabel" the secondary structure affiliated with an amino acid? To do this, I added the class-mean vector for helix to rows representing residues labeled with coil. What nonlinear representation of secondary structure exists after linear erasure, and how is it used?

Table 3 shows how different non-linear probes decode secondary structure representation following linear erasure and class-means ablation. While most nonlinear probes still decode the information, but are meaningfully affected by the linear erasure, QDA remains unaffected throughout. This suggests that the shape of the class cloud, largely untouched by the ablation, closely mirrors that used by the QDA--a tilted ellipsoid. Of note here is that the squares-only reader, which has an untilted ellipsoid shape, falls from 0.81 to 0.56, suggesting further that the orientation of the ellipsoid is an exceptionally significant element of the concept’s representation within the model.

How is this picture shaped by architecture of ESM-2?

ESM-2's bidirectionality within layers (each row reading information from higher and lower rows, representing amino acids flanking it on both sides) affects the difficulty and implementation of concept erasure. What other experiments would teach us more about secondary structural representation in ESM-2?

The most straightforward experiment assesses its scalability--use the exact experimental paradigm across all ESM-2 sizes (8M, 35M, 150M, 650M, 3B and 15B) and see if increased dimensionality affects the shape and nonlinear properties of the concept representation. Furthermore, assessing the boundary conditions of the conclusions, and amending observations about the model's use of coil shape, would involve increasing the usage of DSSP labels to include all 8, and therefore be more granular.
